subject: Physics
title: Statistical Mechanics and Thermodynamics
learningOutcomes: Explain how the motion of gas molecules and their collisions with the walls of the container produce the pressure of a gas.
Derive and use the relation P = mN⟨v²⟩/3V (equivalently P = ⅓ρ⟨v²⟩), where ⟨v²⟩ is the mean-square speed.
Calculate the root mean square speed of gas molecules using v_rms = √(3kT/m) = √(3RT/M) = √(3P/ρ).
Derive and use the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule, ⟨KE⟩ = 3kT/2, and the relation between temperature and kinetic energy.
Illustrate that the ideal gas model is the base from which statistical mechanics emerged, and how it is modified (Van der Waals) for non-ideal gases and for stars.
State that under extreme conditions matter forms degenerate matter (white dwarfs, neutron stars) and Bose-Einstein condensates (superfluidity and superconductivity).

sections.heading: Pressure and the Motion of Gas Molecules
sections.body: The molecules of a gas move rapidly and randomly and collide with one another and with the walls of the container. The collisions with the walls are perfectly elastic, so each molecule rebounds and transfers momentum to the wall. By Newton's second law the rate of transfer of momentum is the force on the wall, and force per unit area is pressure: P = F/A. Decreasing the volume at constant temperature makes the collisions more frequent, so the pressure rises.

sections.heading: Derivation of P = mN⟨v²⟩/3V
sections.body: Take N molecules of mass m in a cube of side l. A molecule with x-velocity v_x1 changes its momentum by −2mv_x1, so the wall receives 2mv_x1. It returns to the same face after covering 2l, so Δt = 2l/v_x1 and the force is F_x1 = mv_x1²/l (Newton's third law). Adding all N molecules gives F_x = (mN/l)⟨v_x²⟩. Random motion makes ⟨v_x²⟩ = ⟨v_y²⟩ = ⟨v_z²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩/3, and pressure is force per area l², so P = mN⟨v²⟩/3V, where V = l³.

sections.heading: Pressure, Density and Kinetic Energy
sections.body: Since mN/V is the density ρ, P = ⅓ρ⟨v²⟩. Writing the number of molecules per unit volume as N₀ = N/V gives P = (2/3)N₀⟨½mv²⟩, so the pressure of a gas is directly proportional to the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules. Comparing PV = (mN/3)⟨v²⟩ with the ideal gas equation PV = NkT (k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, n = N/N_A) gives T = (2/3k)⟨½mv²⟩.

sections.heading: Temperature and Average Translational Kinetic Energy
sections.body: The absolute temperature of an ideal gas is directly proportional to the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules: ⟨½mv²⟩ = 3kT/2. The average kinetic energy therefore depends only on temperature, not on the kind of gas. Temperature, a macroscopic property, is defined by the motion of individual molecules, which is the central idea of statistical mechanics. Always convert Celsius to kelvin with T = t + 273.

sections.heading: Root Mean Square Speed
sections.body: The root mean square speed is the square root of the mean-square speed, v_rms = √[(v₁² + v₂² + … + v_N²)/N], and it is larger than the simple average speed. From ⟨v²⟩ = 3kT/m we get v_rms = √(3kT/m) = √(3RT/M) = √(3P/ρ). It is proportional to √T and inversely proportional to √M, so at the same temperature lighter gases such as hydrogen move much faster than heavier gases such as oxygen (ratio 4:1).

sections.heading: Ideal Gas Model and Statistical Mechanics
sections.body: In the ideal gas model the molecules are treated as points of negligible size with no interactions, and the gas obeys PV = nRT with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. This model governs macroscopic properties such as temperature, pressure, volume and the quantity of gas. Statistical mechanics applies statistics to a very large number of particles and links their microscopic motion to these macroscopic observables, giving thermodynamics its mathematical foundation.

sections.heading: Non-Ideal Gases and the Van der Waals Equation
sections.body: Real gases deviate from PV = nRT at high pressure, high density and low temperature, because the molecules have a finite size and attract one another. Van der Waals treated molecules as hard spheres, replaced V by the effective volume V − nb and P by the effective pressure P + an²/V². The result is (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT, where a and b are empirical constants that differ from gas to gas. At low pressure and high temperature it reduces to the ideal gas equation.

sections.heading: Gravity and Stars
sections.body: At laboratory scale gravity is much weaker than the kinetic energy of the molecules and the pressure of the gas, so it is ignored. On the scale of a star it is essential. In the core of a star the outward pressure from fusion heat, radiation pressure and degeneracy pressure balances the inward pull of gravity; this balance is called hydrostatic equilibrium and keeps the star stable.

sections.heading: Degenerate Matter, White Dwarfs and Neutron Stars
sections.body: Under extremely high pressure gravity squeezes atoms so tightly that the Pauli exclusion principle (two electrons cannot occupy the same quantum state) stops further compression; this is degeneracy pressure and the matter is called degenerate matter. A white dwarf is the remnant of a low- to intermediate-mass star and is held up by electron degeneracy pressure. A neutron star is the remnant of a more massive star in which electrons and protons combine into neutrons; neutron degeneracy pressure balances gravity. It is about 20 km across, about 1.5 solar masses, with density of the order of 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

sections.heading: Bose-Einstein Condensate, Superfluidity and Superconductivity
sections.body: Predicted by Bose and Einstein in the 1920s, a Bose-Einstein condensate forms close to absolute zero when a group of bosons (such as photons, W and Z bosons) occupy the same quantum state. It shows superfluidity (zero viscosity, flow without resistance, persistent vortices) and superconductivity. Superconductivity was discovered by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911 in mercury at 4.2 K; below the critical temperature T_c electrons form boson-like Cooper pairs and the resistance is zero. Examples: Al 1.18 K, Sn 3.72 K, Hg 4.2 K, Pb 7.2 K, a ceramic at 125 K and LaH₁₀ at 250 K (about 170 GPa). Uses: powerful electromagnets, particle accelerators and Maglev trains.

definitions.definition: The force exerted per unit area of a surface.
A collision in which kinetic energy is conserved, so a molecule rebounds from the wall without losing speed.
The average of the squares of the speeds of all the molecules, written ⟨v²⟩.
The square root of the mean-square speed of the molecules.
The arithmetic mean of the speeds of the molecules of a gas.
The number of molecules per unit volume of a gas, N/V.
A gas that obeys the equation PV = nRT, with negligible molecular size and no intermolecular interactions.
A gas whose molecules have a finite size and attract one another, so it deviates from PV = nRT at high pressure and low temperature.
The constant R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ in the ideal gas equation PV = nRT.
The gas constant per molecule, k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
The number of molecules in one mole of a substance, 6.022 × 10²³.
The temperature on the kelvin scale, which is directly proportional to the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules.
The branch of physics that applies statistics to systems of a very large number of particles to link microscopic details with macroscopic observables.
The equation (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT that modifies the ideal gas law for real gases.
The state in which gravity pulling inwards is balanced by the net outward pressure inside a star.
The principle that two electrons cannot occupy the same quantum state.
Matter squeezed by gravity at extremely high pressure so that the Pauli exclusion principle resists further compression.
The pressure that arises from the Pauli exclusion principle and resists further compression of matter.
The remnant of a low- to intermediate-mass star in which gravity is balanced by electron degeneracy pressure.
The remnant of a more massive star in which electrons and protons combine to form neutrons and gravity is balanced by neutron degeneracy pressure.
A particle, such as a photon, W boson or Z boson, that can occupy the same quantum state as other identical particles.
A state of matter formed at extremely low temperature in which a group of bosons occupy the same quantum state.
The flow of a fluid with zero viscosity, without any resistance, at extremely low temperature.
A region in a fluid in which the flow revolves around an axis line.
The sudden disappearance of electrical resistance in a material below its critical temperature.
A pair of electrons in a superconductor that behaves like a boson.
The temperature at and below which the resistivity of a superconducting material becomes zero.
A train that floats above its track by magnetic levitation using powerful superconducting electromagnets.
A bulk property of a system, such as temperature, pressure, volume or entropy, that we measure directly.
The force exerted by the molecule on the wall is equal and opposite to the force exerted by the wall on the molecule.

examTips: Always convert temperature to kelvin first: T = t(°C) + 273. A Celsius value in v_rms, ⟨KE⟩ or PV = nRT is the commonest lost mark.
Do not mix up N (number of molecules) with n (number of moles), or m (mass of ONE molecule) with M (molar mass). Use k with m and N; use R with M and n.
In v_rms = √(3RT/M) the molar mass must be in kg/mol (g/mol ÷ 1000) when R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Learn the three forms: v_rms = √(3kT/m) = √(3RT/M) = √(3P/ρ). Doubling T multiplies v_rms by √2; four times T doubles it.
Remember the derivation chain: Δp = 2mv_x1 → Δt = 2l/v_x1 → F = mv_x1²/l → F_x = (mN/l)⟨v_x²⟩ → ⟨v_x²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩/3 → P = mN⟨v²⟩/3V.
Average translational kinetic energy ⟨KE⟩ = 3kT/2 is the same for every ideal gas at the same temperature; lighter gases are only faster, not more energetic.
Van der Waals: b corrects the volume (V − nb, finite molecular size) and a corrects the pressure (P + an²/V², attraction between molecules).
White dwarf = low- to intermediate-mass star + electron degeneracy pressure; neutron star = more massive star + neutron degeneracy pressure (≈ 20 km, 1.5 M☉, 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³).
Memorise T_c values: Hg 4.2 K, Al 1.18 K, Sn 3.72 K, Pb 7.2 K, ceramic 125 K, LaH₁₀ 250 K; discovery by Onnes in 1911.
Bosons can share a quantum state (BEC); electrons obey the Pauli exclusion principle (degenerate matter). Do not mix the two ideas.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What produces the pressure exerted by a gas on the walls of its container?

options: Collisions of the molecules with the walls
The weight of the gas only

practiceQuestions.explanation: Pressure is the force per unit area produced by the collisions of the gas molecules with the walls.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A molecule of mass m with x-velocity v_x1 collides elastically with a wall. What momentum does the wall receive?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The molecule's momentum changes from mv_x1 to −mv_x1, so the wall receives 2mv_x1.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which expression gives the pressure of an ideal gas?
practiceQuestions.explanation: P = mN⟨v²⟩/3V, equivalent to P = ⅓ρ⟨v²⟩.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The average translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas at absolute temperature T is
The absolute temperature of a gas is made four times. Its rms speed becomes
practiceQuestions.explanation: v_rms ∝ √T, so 4 times T gives √4 = 2 times v_rms.

practiceQuestions.prompt: At the same temperature, the ratio of the rms speed of hydrogen (M = 2) to that of oxygen (M = 32) is
In the Van der Waals equation the term V − nb corrects for

options: The finite size of the molecules

practiceQuestions.explanation: b accounts for the volume occupied by the molecules themselves.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Gravity in a neutron star is balanced by
practiceQuestions.explanation: Neutron degeneracy pressure, arising from the Pauli exclusion principle, balances gravity.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The ideal gas model assumes there are no interactions between the molecules.
practiceQuestions.explanation: In the ideal gas model the molecules have negligible size and no interactions.

practiceQuestions.prompt: At the same temperature, hydrogen molecules have more average translational kinetic energy than oxygen molecules.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. ⟨KE⟩ = 3kT/2 depends only on temperature, so both are equal; hydrogen is only faster.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A superconductor has zero electrical resistance below its critical temperature.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Below T_c the resistivity of a superconductor is zero.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In gas formulas the temperature can be used in degrees Celsius.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Convert to kelvin first: T = t + 273.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The Boltzmann constant is the gas constant per _____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: k = R/N_A is the gas constant per molecule.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The principle that two electrons cannot occupy the same quantum state is called the _____ exclusion principle.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Pauli exclusion principle gives rise to degeneracy pressure.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Mercury becomes a superconductor at a critical temperature of _____ K.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Onnes found the resistance of mercury vanished at 4.2 K in 1911.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the steps in deriving the pressure of an ideal gas in the correct order.

items: A molecule collides elastically with a face of the cubical box
The force on the wall is F_x1 = mv_x1²/l
Using l³ = V gives P = mN⟨v²⟩/3V
The wall receives momentum 2mv_x1 per collision
Adding all N molecules gives F_x = (mN/l)⟨v_x²⟩
Pressure = force ÷ area, with area l²
correctOrder: A molecule collides elastically with a face of the cubical box
The wall receives momentum 2mv_x1 per collision
The force on the wall is F_x1 = mv_x1²/l
Adding all N molecules gives F_x = (mN/l)⟨v_x²⟩
Pressure = force ÷ area, with area l²
Using l³ = V gives P = mN⟨v²⟩/3V

sequencingActivity.explanation: Molecule collides → momentum 2mv_x1 → Δt = 2l/v_x1 → F = mv_x1²/l → sum over N molecules → ⟨v_x²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩/3 → divide by area l² → P = mN⟨v²⟩/3V.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: What is the rms speed of oxygen molecules (M = 32 g/mol) at 27 °C? (R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Gas X has a rms speed of 600 m s⁻¹ at 300 K. At what temperature will its rms speed be 1200 m s⁻¹?
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: v ∝ √T, so doubling v needs 4 times T: 4 × 300 K = 1200 K.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A student uses PV = nRT for a gas at very high pressure and low temperature and gets a poor result. Which reasoning explains this?

options: Gravity is too strong in the laboratory
The molecules have a finite size and attract each other, so V − nb and P + an²/V² are needed
The gas constant R changes with pressure
The temperature cannot be measured in kelvin

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: At high pressure and low temperature molecular size and attraction matter, which the Van der Waals corrections include.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why can a star remain stable as a white dwarf even after all its fusion fuel is used up?

options: Electron degeneracy pressure, from the Pauli exclusion principle, balances gravity
The star becomes a Bose-Einstein condensate
Gravity switches off at high density

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: The Pauli exclusion principle gives electron degeneracy pressure that balances gravity.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Which statement correctly links Cooper pairs, bosons and superconductivity?

options: Electrons repel each other so strongly that resistance doubles
Paired electrons behave like bosons and form a condensate that flows with zero resistance below T_c
Cooper pairs are fermions that obey the Pauli exclusion principle in the same state
Cooper pairs appear only above room temperature

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Below T_c electrons form boson-like Cooper pairs; the condensate flows without resistance.
